title: Exponential expressions: start value and growth factor
keyIdea: In a × bᵗ, a is the start value (the value at t = 0) and b is the factor you multiply by each step. A rise of r% gives b = 1 + r/100, a fall of r% gives b = 1 − r/100: +4% is × 1.04 and −15% is × 0.85.

kid: You put 200 in a bank. Each year the bank adds 5% of what is there. The amount is 200 × 1.05ᵗ after t years.
The 200 is where you start. At t = 0 no years have passed, so you still have 200.
The 1.05 is what you times by each year. You keep all of it, 100%, and get 5% more. That is 105%, or 1.05. You times the new amount each time, so 200 grows by 10, then by 10.50, then by a bit more.
If a thing loses 15% a year, 85% is left. So you times by 0.85 each year, not by 0.15.
adult: An expression a × bᵗ describes a quantity that is multiplied by the same factor b in every time step. At t = 0, b⁰ = 1, so the value is a: the start value. In 500 × 1.04ᵗ the account opens with 500.

The factor compares each step with the one before. A rise of r% keeps the whole amount and adds r%, so b = 1 + r/100 (6% gives 1.06). A fall of r% leaves 100% − r%, so b = 1 − r/100 (15% off gives 0.85). Read backwards, b = 0.92 means a fall of 8% and b = 1.3 a rise of 30%.

Because each percentage is taken of the new amount, the change itself grows or shrinks. 200 × 1.1ᵗ gives 220, 242, 266.2: it doubles after about 7.3 years, while adding a flat 20 a year takes 10. With 0 < b < 1 the losses get smaller each step and the value never reaches 0.

Common mistakes: using r/100 as the factor (0.15 for a 15% fall, which keeps only the lost part); writing 1.6 for 6%; reading the value at t = 1 as the start; working out (a × b)ᵗ instead of a × bᵗ; and adding the first year's change every year, as if the growth were linear.

familyTip: Fold a sheet of paper in half again and again and count the layers: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. That is 1 × 2ᵗ. Then guess how many layers 7 folds would make (128) before you try it.

worked.title: A car is worth 12000 and loses 20% of its value each year. Write its value after t years and find it after 2 years.
steps: Start value: a = 12000, the value now, at t = 0.

practice.prompt: Money in a savings account grows by {r}% each year. What is the growth factor b?
practice.hint: Keep 100% of the money and add {r}%. Turn that total percentage into a decimal.

practice.prompt: A town’s population falls by {r}% each year. What is the decay factor b?
practice.hint: Work out the percentage that is left after the fall, then write it as a decimal.
practice.explain: 100% − {r}% = {=100-r}% is left each year, so b = {=1-r/100}. Using {=r/100} would keep only the part that was lost.

practice.prompt: A colony starts with {a} cells and doubles every hour, so it has {a} × 2ᵗ cells after t hours. How many cells are there after {t} hours?
practice.hint: Work out 2 to the power {t} first: multiply 2 by itself {t} times. Then multiply by {a}.
practice.explain: 2 to the power {t} is {=2**t}, so {a} × {=2**t} = {=a*2**t} cells. Doubling {t} times multiplies the start by {=2**t}.

practice.prompt: A savings balance is 500 × 1.04ᵗ after t years. What does the 1.04 tell you?
choices: The balance grows by 4% each year
The balance grows by 1.04 each year
practice.hint: 1.04 = 104% of the year before. Compare that with 100%.
practice.explain: 1.04 = 100% + 4%, so each year the balance is multiplied by 1.04: it grows by 4%. The start value is 500.

practice.prompt: A pond has 80 fish, and the number falls by 15% each year. Which expression gives the fish after t years?
practice.hint: What percentage of the fish is left after one year?
practice.explain: 85% of the fish are left each year, so b = 0.85 and the expression is 80 × 0.85ᵗ. 0.15 keeps only the lost part, and 1.15 is a rise.

pool.prompt: A plant is {a} mm tall and grows by 5% each week: {a} × 1.05ᵗ. How tall is it at t = 0?
pool.hint: Any number to the power 0 is 1.
pool.explain: 1.05⁰ = 1, so at t = 0 the height is {a} × 1 = {a} mm. That is the start value.

pool.prompt: Each year a value is multiplied by {=1-r/100}. By what percentage does it fall each year?
pool.hint: Turn {=1-r/100} into a percentage, then compare it with 100%.
pool.explain: {=1-r/100} is {=100-r}% of the year before. 100% − {=100-r}% = {r}%, so it falls by {r}% a year.

pool.hint: 1.1² = 1.1 × 1.1. Do the power before you multiply by 200.
pool.explain: 1.1² = 1.21 and 200 × 1.21 = 242. Adding 10% of 200 twice gives 240, which misses the 10% of the first year’s 20.

pool.prompt: Ben says a 15% decrease each year means multiplying by 0.15. What is right?
choices: Multiply by 0.85, the part that is left
pool.hint: After losing 15%, how much of the amount is still there?
pool.explain: Losing 15% leaves 85%, so the factor is 0.85. Multiplying by 0.15 would keep only the 15% that was lost.

pool.prompt: A phone costs 800 and loses 25% of its value each year. What is it worth after 2 years?
pool.hint: The factor is 0.75. Multiply 800 by 0.75 twice.
pool.explain: 800 × 0.75 = 600, then 600 × 0.75 = 450. So 800 × 0.75² = 450. Taking off 200 twice would give 400, which is wrong.

choices: 60 rabbits, and the number goes up by half each year
60 rabbits, and 1.5 more rabbits each year
1.5 rabbits, and the number goes up by 60% each year
pool.hint: 60 is the start. 1.5 = 150% of the year before.
pool.explain: a = 60 is the start and b = 1.5 means 150% of last year: a rise of 50%, or half, each year.

choices: It starts at 1200 and falls by 10% each step
It starts at 1200 and falls by 90% each step
pool.explain: The start value is 1200 and 0.9 = 90% of the step before, so it falls by 10% each step. 1080 is the value at t = 1.

pool.prompt: Which factor means the amount stays the same every year?
pool.hint: What do you multiply a number by to leave it unchanged?
pool.explain: Multiplying by 1 changes nothing, so a × 1ᵗ = a for every t. A factor above 1 grows and a factor between 0 and 1 shrinks.

visual.caption: Does each change make the amount grow or shrink? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: every bar is the one before times b. Set the start value and the factor, turn percentages into factors, and see why multiplying beats adding.
